objectives.en: Explain dynamic method dispatch with a superclass reference
Distinguish overloading (compile time) from overriding (run time)

narration.en: Ask a dog, a cat and a cow to speak: one call, three different sounds. In Java, the object decides at run time which version of a method runs.

body.en: A subclass overrides a method of its superclass by defining a method with the same name, the same parameter list and a compatible return type. The overriding method may not reduce visibility (a public method stays public). static, final and private methods cannot be overridden. The annotation @Override asks the compiler to check that a method really overrides one; a spelling mistake then becomes a compile-time error instead of a silent new method.

points.en: Same name, parameters and return type
final, static, private methods are not overridden

title.en: On the board: dynamic method dispatch

say.en: A superclass reference can refer to a subclass object.
The version that runs depends on the object, not on the reference type.

text.en: Animal a = new Dog();   a.sound();   // Woof

say.en: This is run-time polymorphism. The compiler only checks that Animal has sound().

text.en: Decided at run time by the actual object
Overloading: chosen at compile time by the parameters

narration.en: Let us build up dynamic method dispatch on the board, one step at a time.

tryThis.en: Create a Dog with overriding on. Which version runs?
Turn overriding off for Dog. Which version runs now?
Does the reference type Animal ever decide the version?

label.en: Class whose sound() runs (1 Animal, 2 Dog, 3 Cat)

body.en: Overloading: same name, different parameter lists, usually in the same class; the compiler picks the version from the arguments (compile-time or static polymorphism). Overriding: same signature in a subclass; the JVM picks the version from the actual object (run-time or dynamic polymorphism). A superclass reference can call only the methods declared in the superclass; to call a method that exists only in the subclass, the reference must be cast down: ((Dog) a).fetch().

points.en: Reference type limits which methods can be called
Object type decides which version runs

text.en: Methods differ in their parameter lists
Resolved at run time by the object

explanation.en: Overloading is static polymorphism by parameter lists; overriding is dynamic polymorphism through inheritance.

problem.en: Find the output: class A { void show() { System.out.print("A"); } void call() { show(); } } class B extends A { void show() { System.out.print("B"); } } … A obj = new B(); obj.call();

steps.en: call() is inherited from A and runs.
Inside call(), show() means this.show(), and this is a B object.
